sections.title: Understanding the Problem
points: Internal services use this platform to send immediate notifications, scheduled messages, and campaigns through email, SMS, or push providers.
Request acceptance, provider acceptance, and recipient delivery are different events. Record their states separately.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
points: An upstream service can request an immediate or future notification.
An upstream service can send a campaign to a defined user segment.
Users can set channel opt-outs and quiet hours. Template authoring and delivery analytics are outside the core scope.

sections.title: Non-functional Requirements
points: Provide at-least-once delivery attempts with best-effort deduplication. Confirm acceptance only after durable storage or queue acknowledgement.
The scenario has surges near 5,000 notifications per second. High-priority messages should reach the provider within about five seconds.
Provider outages and repeated queue delivery must not lose accepted work. The system can reduce duplicates but cannot eliminate every duplicate.

sections.title: Core Entities
points: Notification identifies one user, channel, content, priority, schedule, stable ID, and outcome.
Campaign contains the segment, message or template, schedule, and expansion progress. Segment identifies the recipient membership.
User contains contact details, device tokens, and preferences. Delivery attempts record provider identifiers and responses.

sections.title: API
points: POST /notifications accepts the recipient, content, channel, priority, optional schedule, and idempotency key.
POST /campaigns accepts a segment, template, schedule, and idempotency key. It returns the accepted campaign ID.
PUT /users/{userId}/preferences replaces preferences. GET /notifications/{id} returns the recorded outcome. Device registration updates rotating push tokens.
Authenticate the sending service and its authority over the recipient. Internal callers can supply user IDs after performing their own authorization.

sections.title: 1) Immediate and scheduled delivery
points: The initial Notification Service stores a pending row and calls the provider directly. It then records the provider's response.
Email uses an address, SMS uses a phone number, and push uses a device token. APNs and FCM maintain device connections.
A future request remains scheduled in the database. The Scheduler Cron finds due rows and sends them through the delivery path.
The durability deep dive moves immediate delivery to workers. After that change, the API reports acceptance before a provider result exists.

flows.title: Send directly in the initial design
steps: The upstream service sends the recipient, channel, and content through the API Gateway.
The Notification Service reads the recipient's address. It writes a pending notification row.
The service calls the email provider. It records the provider's response as sent or failed.
The service returns the notification ID and result. This initial sequence does not recover every crash safely.

flows.title: Send a scheduled notification
steps: The Notification Service stores a future notification with its scheduled time.
The Scheduler Cron queries scheduled rows whose time has arrived.
It sends each due notification through the delivery path. The later durable design enqueues this work instead of calling providers inline.
The system records progress with a stable notification ID. Repeated scheduling must refer to the same logical notification.

sections.title: 2) Campaign expansion
points: Store the campaign before returning its ID. At the scheduled time, the Scheduler Cron reads a snapshot of the segment membership.
Expand the snapshot into bounded recipient batches. Keep a cursor so a restart can continue the expansion.
Derive a stable notification ID from the campaign and user IDs. Repeated expansion then identifies the same logical sends.
The initial loop shares capacity with direct sends. The priority deep dive separates bulk work from urgent delivery.

flows.title: Expand a campaign's recipient snapshot
steps: The Notification Service stores a campaign with a stable ID and returns acceptance.
When the campaign is due, the Scheduler Cron reads a snapshot of its segment membership.
It creates a notification for each recipient. Each notification uses the campaign and user IDs as its stable identity.
The cron records expansion progress after each bounded batch. A restart resumes or safely repeats that batch.
The final design sends campaign work to the standard queue. Campaign completion and recipient delivery remain separate states.

sections.title: 3) Preferences
points: Store opt-outs, quiet hours, and timezone with user data. Any preference cache needs an explicit freshness rule.
Check preferences immediately before the provider call. A user can opt out after a campaign was created.
Record suppression with its reason. Apply the product's rules for high-priority messages and quiet hours consistently.

sections.title: 1) Do not lose accepted work
points: The source's improved immediate path writes directly to a durable queue. SQS acknowledgement is the acceptance boundary for that request.
A worker receives the message, checks preferences, calls the provider, and records the outcome in PostgreSQL. It then deletes the message.
A failed worker leaves the message available for retry after its visibility timeout. Repeated failures enter a dead-letter queue.
Scheduled requests and campaigns remain in the database until due. Their publisher needs recoverable progress and stable notification IDs.
A separate database write followed by queue publication can fail between operations. An outbox fits when both operations must commit together.
Track queued age and state changes. A retained but stuck message still needs detection and recovery.

flows.title: Accept through a durable queue and deliver
steps: The Notification Service validates an immediate request and writes it to SQS with a stable notification ID.
SQS acknowledges durable receipt. The service returns 202 and the notification ID.
A worker receives the message. It checks contact details and current preferences.
The worker calls the provider if delivery is allowed. It records the outcome or suppression in PostgreSQL.
The worker deletes the queue message only after recording the result. A crash before deletion permits redelivery.
Temporary failures retry with delay. Repeated failures move to a dead-letter queue for inspection.

sections.title: 2) Priority and provider capacity
points: Separate high-priority and standard queues. Reserve a worker pool for urgent notifications so slow bulk calls cannot occupy all workers.
Reserve part of each provider's rate budget for high-priority work. Redis token buckets can enforce the shared budget.
Apply tenant quotas as needed. A campaign must not consume every provider token available to urgent messages.
During provider failure, use bounded retries and a circuit breaker. Limit simultaneous calls to each provider.
A provider router can select a supported fallback. A complete provider outage can still break the delivery-time target.

flows.title: Protect an urgent send during a campaign
steps: The Notification Service routes urgent work to the High Priority Queue. Campaign work enters the Standard Queue.
A worker from the reserved urgent pool receives the high-priority notification.
The worker obtains a provider token from the reserved Redis budget. Standard workers cannot spend that reserved allocation.
The worker checks preferences and calls the provider. It records the result before acknowledging the queue message.

sections.title: 3) Duplicate prevention
points: Derive notification IDs from stable caller keys. Campaign creation also needs a stable key, or retried campaigns produce new recipient IDs.
Check recent successful sends in Redis before delivery. On a cache miss, the durable outcome can confirm an earlier successful send.
Record a successful outcome and store its ID in the cache only after provider acceptance. A permanent claim before sending can lose work after a crash.
Two concurrent attempts can still race. A lost provider response also leaves an uncertain outcome that local state cannot fully resolve.
Use provider idempotency or status lookup when available. Otherwise, define the duplicate-risk policy and retain at-least-once semantics.

flows.title: Check a completed send before redelivery
steps: A worker receives a notification with the same stable ID as an earlier attempt.
It checks the Redis success cache. If necessary, it checks the durable successful outcome.
If success exists, the worker skips the provider call. Otherwise, it sends and records the resulting outcome.
After provider acceptance and outcome storage, it adds the ID to the success cache.
A crash after provider acceptance can still cause a duplicate. Provider idempotency or status lookup can reduce this uncertain case.

sections.title: Final Design
points: Immediate requests enter durable priority queues. Scheduled notifications and campaign batches enter the same path when they become due.
Separate worker pools and provider budgets protect urgent traffic. Workers check preferences and record sent, failed, or suppressed outcomes.
Stable IDs and a Redis success cache reduce duplicates. Provider-aware retries and explicit uncertain outcomes support recovery.
